name: tine electric piano
title: Electric piano (tine)
builder: struck, partials (1.0 ring 3.0 s, 2.0 level 0.25, 7.1 level 0.3 ring 0.25 s), mallet 0.02 at 2 kHz (unchanged)
notes: Range kept (rule 6): Fender Rhodes page gives '54, 73 or 88 keys' and a Piano Bass of 'E1-B3' (the only note names on the page), so E1-E7 for 73 keys (six octaves and a note) is consistent; no fetched source gives the 73-key ends in note names, nor shows E1-E7 wrong. Sound, Fender Rhodes page: 'the hammers strike thin metal tines, which vibrate next to an electromagnetic pickup'; 'Vibrating tines produce a mellower timbre'; tine and tone bar together give 'a characteristic "bell" sound'

name: reed electric piano
title: Electric piano (reed)
builder: plucked falling_series(16, 6 dB per octave), ring 2.0 s, drive 1.5, low pass 4 kHz (unchanged)
notes: Range confirmed by the Wurlitzer electric piano page: 'Most Wurlitzers are 64-note instruments', running 'from A an octave above the lowest note' of an 88-key piano to C an octave below its top note, i.e. A1 to C7. Sound, same page: 'striking a metal reed with a felt hammer', an electrostatic pickup; 'closer to a sawtooth wave' than a Rhodes; played hard an overdriven 'bark'

name: clavinet
title: Clavinet
builder: plucked plucked_series(28, 2 dB per octave, pluck position 0.06), ring 1.0 s, high pass 150 Hz, drive 0.8 (unchanged)
notes: Range confirmed by the Hohner Clavinet page: 'Most models have 60 keys ranging from F1 to E6'. Sound, same page: 'a harp of 60 tensioned steel strings', each key's rubber pad frets its string, an electromagnetic pickup (two sets on most models)

name: hohner pianet
title: Hohner Pianet
builder: plucked falling_series(12, 9 dB per octave), ring 1.2 s, release 0.15, no drive, low pass 3 kHz (to be tuned by ear; sources give no numbers)
notes: Range, Hohner Pianet page: 'The original design had "61 keys ranging from F1 to F6 (43.6 Hz - 1396.9 Hz)"'; later models dropped the top F, leaving 60 keys (the original compass is used). Sound, same page: a pad 'adheres to the reed when at rest' and lifts away when the key is pressed (the reed is released, not hammered); early models read it with 'variable capacitance'; 'the initial strike produces a complex mixture of harmonics, which then settles into a cleaner tone'. Differs from reed electric piano (hammer-struck, driven, bark): no drive, a brighter attack that mellows within the note (harmonics fall faster than the fundamental), shorter ring. The page names no click level, so no pad click is built

name: wurlitzer electronic piano
title: Wurlitzer electronic piano
notes: Audit spelling 'wurlitzer electronic piano'. Wurlitzer electric piano page: sound by 'striking a metal reed with a felt hammer' read by an electrostatic pickup; the same build as the catalog reed electric piano (struck steel reed, pickup, sawtooth-like, 'bark'); 64 notes A1-C7 as the reed electric piano's range

name: hohner clavinet
title: Hohner Clavinet
notes: Audit spelling 'hohner clavinet'. Hohner Clavinet page: the Clavinet is Hohner's instrument (seven models, 1964 to 1982), 'most models have 60 keys ranging from F1 to E6', the catalog clavinet's range; the maker's name is the only difference

name: hammond b3
title: Hammond B-3 (with Leslie)
waits_for: a pitch and amplitude LFO (the Leslie rotating speaker and the scanner vibrato)
notes: Hammond organ page: the B-3 and C-3 'were introduced with the additional harmonic percussion feature' (the page dates them 1954; the audit's 1955 appears only in the price box); the T series 'did include the scanner-vibrato as seen on the B-3'. The identifying sound is the Leslie: 'Sound is emitted by a rotating horn over a stationary treble compression driver' and 'The Doppler effect from the moving sources creates the constantly shifting pitch'. Without the Leslie it is the catalog tonewheel organs (drawbars and percussion), which are MOVE rows here

name: telharmonium
title: Telharmonium (Dynamophone)
notes: Telharmonium page: 'Each rheotome was actually a cog with a specific number of notched teeth'; the instrument had '153 keys'; 'Cahill added several extra tonewheels to add harmonics to each note'; tones 'clear and pure'. The page gives the key count but no lowest or highest note ('eight separate taps off the output shifted the frequency to different octaves' is the only octave sentence); the audit's C1-C7 was not sourced

name: yamaha cp electric grand
title: Yamaha CP electric grand
builder: none yet (struck strings, piezo pickup, no soundboard)
notes: Yamaha CP-70 page: '73 keys (CP-70, CP-70B)' and '88 keys (CP-80)'; 'piezo-electric pickups mounted on the harp casting', 'no soundboard', 'the same piano action as an acoustic instrument'. No note names on the page, so no range from a source; it is a struck-string piano with pickups, so on SHIP it would also need a build that differs from grand piano

name: mellotron
title: Mellotron
notes: Mellotron page: each key's tape is 'pushed against a playback head', and a spring pulls it back; infobox '1 or 2 x 35 note manuals (G2-F5)' (the M300 is a '52-note single manual'); replay has 'minor fluctuations in pitch'. The sound is the recorded instruments on tape, which the engine cannot play back (an oscillator imitation would be another instrument's sound). Range G2-F5 is sourced for when it ships

name: chamberlin
title: Chamberlin
waits_for: sample playback and a sourced range
notes: Audit spelling 'chamberlin' (in keyboards.md and electronic.md). Chamberlin page: 'an electro-mechanical keyboard instrument that was a precursor to the Mellotron'; 'Underneath each key is a tape-playing mechanism'. Not an alias: the page and the Mellotron page treat them as two instruments (Mellotron 'evolved from the similar Chamberlin'); the page gives no key count or range

name: optigan
title: Optigan
waits_for: sample playback and a sourced range
notes: Optigan page: 'standard three-octave piano-style keyboard'; light passes through 'spinning 12-inch clear discs' read by photodiodes; 37 single-note tracks and 21 chord tracks; 'poor tonal quality'; tempo changes the pitch. The sound is the recorded discs (no replay in the engine); the page gives no note names for the three octaves

name: vako orchestron
title: Vako Orchestron
waits_for: sample playback and a sourced range
notes: Orchestron page: 'each note of the keyboard is recorded onto a short, looped track on a pre-recorded, interchangeable optical disc'; 'the professional version of the Mattel Optigan'; 'low fidelity'. The page does not specify the keyboard's range. Not an alias of optigan (a separate product, with higher-fidelity outer disc rings)

name: welte lichttonorgel
title: Welte Lichttonorgel
waits_for: sample playback and a sourced range
notes: 120years.net: '12 glass disks, each printed with 18 different looped waveforms'; photoelectric cells read them; the sounds were 'photographically drawn "recordings" of different models of famous organs'. The page states no keyboard range; the audit's C2-C7 was from memory

name: rhodes piano bass
title: Rhodes piano bass
notes: Fender Rhodes page: a '32-note keyboard bass approximating the string bass's range (E1-B3)', the same tine and tone-bar generator ('The tone generator assembly acts as a tuning fork'). No fetched source gives it a different construction or sound, and the catalog tine electric piano (E1-E7) already covers E1-B3, so it would build the same instrument and no game would ask for it by name

name: rhodes celeste
title: Fender Rhodes Celeste
notes: Fender Rhodes page: the Celeste 'used the top three or four octaves, respectively, of the Fender Rhodes piano': the same tines, only the high ones, no note names given. The catalog tine electric piano covers that register, so it would build the same instrument and no game would ask for it by name

name: oramics
title: Oramics
notes: Oramics page: 'drawing on 35mm film strips to control the sound produced', the film masks light to photocells, 'the output from the machine was monophonic'; no keyboard. One studio machine played by drawn film, not by note, so there is no pitched instrument to give a range and no game would ask for it by name. Electronic sound synthesis (H-S 53)

name: solovox
title: Solovox
notes: Hammond organ page (the Solovox URL redirects there): the Solovox's generator uses 'a vacuum tube oscillator and octave divider circuits originally designed for Novachord'; 'a three-octave mini keyboard'. Vacuum-tube oscillators, so H-S 53 (electronic), not this batch; matched the audit filter on a word in passing

name: vox continental
title: Vox Continental
notes: Vox Continental page: 'The organ's sound comes from twelve oscillators' with frequency dividers, 'relatively unstable germanium transistors'; the infobox lists 'Synthesis type' as 'Electronic'. H-S 53, not this batch; the catalog combo organ covers the sound

name: dx7 ep
title: DX7 electric piano
notes: Yamaha DX7 page: 'Digital linear frequency modulation', 'the first successful digital synthesizer'; the 'E Piano 1' preset imitates a Rhodes-style piano. A synthesizer preset (H-S 53), not an electromechanical instrument; it is also an FM sound the engine cannot make

name: wurlitzer sideman
title: Wurlitzer Sideman
notes: Drum machine page: 'In 1959, [Wurlitzer] released the Side Man', which 'generates sounds mechanically by a rotating disc, similar to a music box', with a tempo slider of 34 to 150 beats per minute. A rhythm machine of preset patterns, unpitched, not an instrument played by note; drum voices belong to drums and percussion

name: kinura
title: Kinura
notes: Audit: a theatre organ reed stop ('thin buzzing tone'), existence and range unverified. A pipe-organ stop, so organs, not electromechanical; it matched the audit filter only on a word in passing

name: band organ
title: Band organ
notes: Fairground organ page: a band organ is the US name for a fairground organ, wind 'from mechanically powered bellows', book or roll music. A pneumatic mechanical organ, not electromechanical (matched the filter on a word in passing); the mechanical-instruments tag covers it with the organs
